editorial.headline: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A foreign investor cannot register this wholesale activity in Bali today, even though it is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership across every business scale.
editorial.body:
At its centre, this is a broad wholesale category for products not otherwise included in the preceding wholesale groupings. Its expressly stated examples move from textile fibre and precious stones—diamonds, gems, sapphires and others—to e-liquid for electronic cigarettes. They also include wooden packaging in the form of boxes, crates, drums and similar forms, as well as wooden cable reels, pallets and other wooden transport boards. What joins these lines is not a single material or customer market, but their placement within this residual wholesale field. The scope should therefore be read for the products it expressly names, rather than as a shortcut for a narrower specialty trade.

The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses. That is the complete scale range given in the record, which does not narrow the category to a particular enterprise size. At the national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical ownership terms, the national record permits a foreign investor to hold the entire stake. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The point is straightforward: the national setting is not a partial-ownership exception; the listed ceiling is full foreign ownership.

That clarity is undone in Bali. A foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA in Bali today. It is marked BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO: the OSS assessment at the Besar scale is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every stated scope, and the record says this triggers Bali’s moratorium. The island-wide, permanent provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The stated block is tied to the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026, and cites Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.

This creates a precise, not paradoxical, reading. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA with a 100% ceiling and across all four named business scales. In Bali, however, that national position does not produce a PMA registration path, because its large-scale OSS risk classification falls inside the province’s permanent moratorium. Anyone evaluating the activity for a Bali establishment needs to treat those statements as simultaneous: full national foreign-ownership openness on one hand, and a current Bali PMA block on the other.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the activity is open to PMA with a 100% ceiling; in Bali, it has no PMA registration path.
